What special assistance is the federal government giving to areas designated as rural development areas under ARDA?

1.	Under the new Federal-Provincial Rural Development Agreement now being signed with the provinces, special assistance is provided to Rural Development Areas and to Special Rural Development Areas under two Parts of the Agreement.
Rural Development Areas are rural areas jointly agreed to by the federal Minister and the provincial Minister, which are subject to low income, underemployment, and other disadvantage. Normally, they are areas where over 50 per cent of the families have incomes of less than $3,000 per year. In such areas Canada will share half the cost of land development enterprises, including forest stand improvement on Crown or other public authority forest land; the provision of financial or other assistance to farm or wood-lot operators to undertake recreation and wildlife projects on existing holdings; the development on existing farms in need of special assistance of land now unimproved but suitable for agriculture for the purpose of increasing the efficiency of the farm operation; the undertaking of primary fisheries development projects not provided for in other federal or federal-provincial programs consistent with the intent of the program; the development of the tourist industry through the provision of public recreation areas including basic infrastructure facilities in conformity with an overall plan.
In addition, Canada will make a grant to a Province based on $3 per rural family in Rural Development Areas for projects to increase income and employment opportunities in cases where such projects are not allowed elsewhere in the ARDA Agreement.
Special Rural Development Areas are areas jointly recognized which are subject to widespread low income; have major adjustment problems, and have recognized development potentials. They are recognized after research
June 2, 1965

has been done in these areas; a comprehensive development plan has been drawn, and a special program agreement entered into to implement the development program. These agreements allow tor projects provided for elsewhere in the ARDA Federal-Provincial Rural Development Agreement, including programs for research, land use and farm adjustment, rehabilitation, soil and water conservation, and so on; projects allowed for in Rural Development Areas, and in addition major developmental projects under the Comprehensive Plan.
These major developmental projects may be financed from a special $50 million Fund for Rural Economic Development provided for in the Agreement.
In addition, the federal government is financing the full cost of research and studies in one area in each province leading to the drawing of a development plan.

This article states that China has the right to support North Viet Nam; that North Viet Nam has, and always has had the right to
June 2, 1965

support the Viet Cong in the south, and that North Viet Nam is free to cease to be restricted by the military demarcation line, the 17th parallel, which was provided for in the 1954 Geneva agreement.
I would express doubt, in view of the contentions made in the past six weeks by the North Vietnamese, that they would be prepared to publicly support such a position. Yesterday I asked our High Commissioner in London to call on the Foreign Secretary to discuss a number of matters, and I see there has been public mention that among the matters discussed was the Cambodian question. I have not seen the statement made by the ambassador. I suspect he was referring to the discussions which are now under way at the United Nations in the committee of 33. Mr. Speaker, my remarks will have a self-imposed time allocation of not more than 15 minutes and perhaps less. I want to deal with one particular aspect of the debate.
There seems to be a recurring theme in the speeches of members of the Conservative and Liberal parties about the good old days when there were two parties in the House, that the House was designed for two parties and that it would be wonderful if this were the way it could operate. It has been a very long time since that has been the case in Canada. In fact the last election which returned two parties to this House was that of 1917, and possibly it was only one and a half parties at that time because half of the Liberal party was in the Union Government of the day.
I think we should be reminded periodically that following 1917 there was the election of 1921 which returned 117 Liberals, 59 Conservatives, 64 Progressives, 3 Labour and 1 Independent. The 1925 election returned 101 Liberals, 116 Conservatives, 24 Progressives, 2 Labour and 2 Independents.
In 1926 we had large third and fourth groups, that election having returned 116 Liberals, 91 Conservatives, 11 United Farmers of Alberta, 13 Progressives, 9 Liberal-Progressives, 3 Labour and 2 Independents. In 1930 there were 137 Conservatives, 88 Liberals, 10 United Farmers, 2 Progressives, 3 Liberal-Progressives, 2 Labour, 1 Independent Labour and 2 Independents. In 1935 there were 171 Liberals and 39 Conservatives.
Indeed, for the benefit of the hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Nugent), I would point out that in the Parliaments of 1935 and 1940 there were only 39 Conservative Members. The hon. Member talked about setting a high limit on what should be considered a party. I point out that his party shrunk to 39 on two occasions and to 41 on another. It could happen again next year. In any event in 1935 the figures were 171 Liberals, 39 Conservatives, 17 Social Credit, 7 C.C.F., 5 Independent Liberals, 2 Liberal-Progressives, 1 Independent Conservative, 1 Reconstruction, 1 Independent and 1 U.F.O. In the Parliament of 1940 there were 184 Liberals, 39 Conservatives, 10 Social Credit representatives, 8 members of the C.C.F. party and a number of others called Liberal Progressives, Independent Liberals, Independent Conservatives, Independent, and so on.

[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Throughout the years ever since the election of 1921 there have been third or fourth parties or a large number of independent members. So it is a long time since we have had a straight two-party system in Canada and I suggest the situation will not change in a hurry.
Some Members have put forward the view that changes in the rules would encourage the multiplication of parties. That is nonsense. It has nothing to do with the rules of this House but concerns rather dissatisfaction with the policies followed by existing parties. The fact that the Social Credit party elected a great many Members to this House from Quebec in 1962 and 1963 had nothing whatever to do with rules of the House of Commons. Electors will vote for the candidates who appeal to them regardless of what our rules are here.
Yesterday the hon. Member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) referred to the question of the definition of parties. We have made some progress in this direction during the last two years in this House, particularly in 1963. The hon. lady mentioned the practice in the National Assembly of France. I am partial to this idea though I do not think we can realize it quickly in Canada. Nevertheless it needs further exploration and study. It is useless to carry on the pretence that political parties do not exist, as is done in many of our rules and, indeed, in the Elections Act itself. Parties do exist. Most of us would not be here were it not for the support of the political parties of which we are Members. People would not vote for us as independents. The role played by the parties in elections and in the operation of Parliament should receive further recognition. I realize this presents difficulties but we have made a beginning by recognizing the existence of more than two parties.
For a long time in Canada, indeed, for nearly 45 years, there have been more than two parties in the House of Commons. Taking into account the fact that parties have been recognized by the rules of the House since 1963, I believe that many of the arguments put forward during this debate by representatives of the Official Opposition particularly fall to the ground. We should recognize now that there is every possibility that as a result of any future election there will be other parties represented in this House beside the Official Opposition.

I think we have had ample discussion on this point now. This was not part of the motion presented to us by the Government for consideration, though it is an important question. I think the House might well consider striking a special committee composed of Members of the type who made up the committee on the rules under Mr. Speaker to consider this question. I do not think we can accomplish very much by discussing it now, particularly if we bring personalities into the subject.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all of us realize that some changes in the rules and procedures of the House are necessary from time to time in order to meet changing conditions. However, it is a fallacy to think that rule changes alone will make Parliament into a more efficient and smoother operating institution. What in my opinion is much more important is the attitude taken by Members of Parliament and by all parties in the House, their sense of responsibility or otherwise, their willingness to observe the rules or to flout them.
These are essentially the things which make this institution run reasonably well or prevent it from doing so. I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) looking up with interest at this point. He knows from his personal experience that this is the case. The system under which we have been operating worked much better during the first ten years after the war than it has during the past ten years. I think there is no doubt about that. This is in spite of the fact that particularly in the first part of this 20 year period a considerable number of rule changes were put into effect. All those changes were designed to save the time of the House to some extent. For exam-
House of Commons Procedures pie, there was the limitation placed on the length of the debate on the Address and on the Budget debate. Despite those measures the length of our sessions has not been shortened.
Some will say this is because there was less business to be done in Parliament during the decade that followed the war than there is at the present time. I submit this is not really the case. I believe there was more business before the House then, more measures of various kinds to be considered in the immediate post-war sessions than has ever been the case in any similar period of time since then. Nevertheless, we got through all our business more expeditiously than in recent years.
Again, some will say that the difficulties of the past few years have been due primarily to the multiplicity of parties in the House. This factor has undoubtedly contributed to the length of time taken on various matters. More time has been taken by speakers commenting on statements made by Ministers on the orders of the day, as well as during the question period and in the various debates. I think the multiplicity of parties is unquestionably one of the reasons rule changes have been discussed as much as they have been discussed; it is one of the reasons most of us are looking toward some changes in the rules at the present time. However, once again I do not believe it is the basic reason for our present difficulties.
I would point out that in 1945 there were actually more parties in the House than there are at the present time. A Liberal Government was in power with a bare majority. In opposition were the Conservative party, the C.C.F., the Social Credit group, the Bloc Populaire, the Communist party and a considerable number of independents. It is true there were only four parties officially or semi-officially recognized. Nevertheless these other parties existed. Therefore the present situation with five parties in the House, or a multiplicity of parties, is not new to us, as pointed out by the last speaker.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The real reason that things do not move more smoothly than they do in this Chamber and were better, let us say, in the period 10 to 20 years ago is that in that period the rules were observed much more and there was a greater spirit of co-operation than now exists and has existed during recent years. During that period we did not have the constant raising of points of order and questions of privilege which has distinguished nearly every day's sitting of recent date. We
June 2, 196S

House of Commons Procedures did not have constant challenges of Speaker's rulings, which I think have done much to impair the authority of the Speaker and thus have made it more difficult to maintain order in the Chamber and to prevent a great deal of wasting of time.
Essentially, Mr. Speaker, what all this boils down to is that this institution is and will be what its Members make it. If Members show that sense of responsibility and selfdiscipline which is essential for the proper functioning of a democratic assembly, then the rule changes which are proposed will not be of too much importance and, in fact, within the rules under which we are at present operating we could continue without any undue difficulty.
This leads me, Mr. Speaker, directly into the few remarks I should like to make regarding the proposed limitation of the time taken by the daily question period. I think the proposal to limit this period to half an hour provides sufficient time, provided, and this is important, that certain conditions are met. The first of those conditions is that the questions themselves be short and within the rules. In recent years, particularly during the past five or six years, we have had more questions asked which were not within the rules than those which were within the rules. In particular, the custom has developed more and more of asking extremely long and involved questions, in fact of making statements rather than putting questions. If the question period is to be limited to half an hour, I think it is absolutely essential that the rules in regard to oral questions be strictly observed and that the Speaker be in a position to see that they are strictly observed.
The corollary of that, which is just as important, is that the answers given by Ministers must also be short and within the rules. We had an example today of what happens when this is not the case. I know from my own experience that there is always a temptation for Ministers to smuggle in, supposedly as an answer to a question, what should be put forward as a statement. I have done that myself and it has been done, I think, during the entire 20 years I have been here.
However, when there is no limitation on the length of time taken by the question period this is not so important. It is not a good practice but nevertheless it is not so crucial. But if there is to be a limitation of the question period this practice must be done away with absolutely; otherwise the rights of all Members of the House in regard to the

opportunity to ask questions are seriously impaired. So I hope that if this new rule does come into effect this is one of the conditions that Your Honour or whoever is sitting in your seat will ensure is observed. Ministers should not try to make long statements in answer to questions.
There is another point I wish to make. If this limitation is to work properly it is essential that written questions be answered promptly. This matter was raised today and also yesterday. There are a number of questions on the order paper today which have been there for a long period of time. Since the session started on April 5 some nine pages of questions have accumulated which appear on today's order paper and were placed there in the month of April. Yet here it is June 2nd and these questions are still unanswered. A further 15 pages of questions were put on the order paper between the beginning of May and May 15 and none of these questions has been answered. There is also a large number of questions which have been put down following that date.
I submit that if Members were able to receive prompt answers to the questions they put on the order paper they would not ask or feel it necessary to ask nearly as many oral questions as they do. If the Government is not prepared to answer written questions within a reasonable length of time, then once more this will prevent the satisfactory operation of a half hour limitation for the daily question period. I suggest that in answering these questions a limit of seven days should be imposed, that is to say, one full week from the time the question first appears on the order paper. If it has not been answered within that length of time then the Minister concerned should be required to give an explanation.

I think that when we are making changes in our rules and providing for a maximum question period per day of half an hour this is one of the matters which will have to be taken into consideration and dealt with at the same time. There is one other condition in connection with questions which I think is essential if this half hour limitation is to work satisfactorily and that is that on one day a week the length of the question period should not be limited to half an hour. This would enable some of the backbenchers particularly, who perhaps have difficulty being seen by the Speaker, to have the opportunity on at least one day a week to put their questions. I think we in this House all want to be fair about these things, but it does seem to me that if the various conditions I have mentioned so far as questions are concerned were put into effect they would bring about a situation where a half hour question period four days per week would work satisfactorily and at the same time no member would be in a position where it would become impossible for him to put a question and receive an answer.

I should now like to deal with what I think is undoubtedly the most important change proposed and that is the allocation of time for debate. Nearly all of us recognize that some half way house is required between nothing and closure under the situation which now exists. When the Government introduced this proposal the change did not represent a half way house but something more like a three-quarter or four-fifth-way house. That proposal was too extreme and the Government recognized that fact. It has now proposed that there should be a minimum period for each stage of a debate, and that is undoubtedly a considerable improvement.
There is one thing in connection with this matter which should be fully understood and that is that the minimum period provided for each stage of debate should not automatically be considered as the period to be adopted every time an allocation of time is brought in. I think it must be realized that a variation in the amount of time required for debate is inevitable and that in all fairness the debate in respect of some subjects will require a greater length of time. That is an essential element in the allocation of time rule. The minimum period allowed should not under any circumstances be looked upon as the amount of time to be provided on each and every occasion that this rule is invoked. A firm assurance on the part of the Government along this line would do a great deal to reassure a considerable number of us in respect of this whole matter.
If my understanding is correct, the allocation of time would be put into effect before any debate on any subject began. One thing that should be provided is a minimum period during which debate would take place before any allocation of time was put into effect. That again would go a long way toward reassuring many Members in this House in respect of this matter.
One of the reasons the Opposition parties in the House and the Canadian public generally were so concerned about the application of closure during the pipe line debate was that closure was imposed before the debate at several stages of that measure had started. If a minimum period for debate were provided in order to keep away from that kind of a situation before the allocation of time was or could be applied, this would provide a safeguard.

I think most of us are prepared to agree that something should be done to change that situation but we are not agreeable to something which is too extreme. The Government realized that what it proposed at the beginning was too extreme. We have now had various safeguards suggested and I am suggesting another one which I think would be advantageous.
The hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) suggested that there should be a week between second reading and the committee stage and a week between the committee stage and third reading. I think that is a sound idea. It is my understanding that some Members on the Government side of the House have agreed

I would hope the Government would move in that direction. I think one of the things we have to realize is that any limitation of time for debate runs into the basic difficulty that the right of every Member to be heard in this House, if he wishes to be heard, is impaired or in fact destroyed. Therefore our study really has to be with regard to how we can preserve the individual Member's rights in that respect to the greatest degree possible and at the same time introduce something which will serve to enable the time of the House to be allocated in a more reasonable manner than has often been the case in the past.
Once more, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that this difficulty can be met to some extent at least by extending the hours of sitting, even so far as to sit all night if necessary in some cases. This is a matter which one or two other Members have mentioned. I think in most cases this would provide the opportunity for any Member who really wanted to speak and had not had the opportunity to do so to make his contribution to the debate. This would be particularly essential, I believe, in the committee stage of any bill with regard to which there was an allocation of time. As a result of extending the sitting hours and having an all night session if required, it would be possible for each of the clauses of the bill to be dealt with and at the same time it would provide the necessary opportunity for every Member who had not been heard up to that point to have his say in regard to the matter which especially concerned him and which was to be found in one of the clauses. I believe this is something we will have to look into. It might impose a very considerable strain if the hours of sitting were extended and there were a number of evenings when we in fact sat very much longer hours. The strain might be greater than was the case, at the time of the automatic adjournment at eleven o'clock, which was in effect for years after I first came to this House, and latterly since the ten o'clock adjournment came into effect.

amendment and subamendment now before the House, I may say I feel it is reasonable that when you allocate time for a measure there should be a limitation on the length of the speeches. I believe you have to make an exception with regard to the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Dief-enbaker) and also at second reading stage, particularly when a bill is introduced by a Minister. Frequently, if a bill is complex in nature the Minister introducing it is bound to have to take more than 20 minutes to explain it properly. It is only reasonable that under those circumstances the people I have mentioned should have a longer period. I would have no objection to having a limitation of say an hour for the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition or a Minister introducing a piece of legislation. But the remainder of the Members of the House should be limited to 20 minutes so that an opportunity would be given to as many as possible to have their say on a piece of legislation which, by its nature, would be contentious or otherwise there would not be an allocation of time for it.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks to make. The hon. Member for Calgary North (Mr. Harkness) has said that the Government, if it wishes to invoke closure, has the power to do so under rule 33. Frankly, a lot of this talk about allocation of time is really a refusal to face up to the responsibility of invoking rule 33. The guillotine has now come into operation, and I would say it came in wrapped with a flag because this seems to have been the motivation respecting a good many of the proposals which have come forward and about which we heard earlier.
I should like to make an appeal to the Government with regard to the proposed rule changes contained in paragraph 1 of order No. 14. Since these have now been amended in such a way as to be acceptable to the House, I suggest that we take out paragraph 10 of order No. 15, which deals with a revised Standing Order 65, and make a minor adjustment in Standing Order 65 which I have suggested to the Leader of the House, namely, that in the fifth line of the first paragraph the words "with all con-

venient speed" should be replaced by the words, "within 10 sitting days after it is appointed". In other words, the striking committee will have to report earlier, which would guarantee that the committees would be set up earlier.
I have previously spoken about the lack of guarantee of action to institute the committees and get them going. Personally I think the Government proposal is weak and that such an amendment would strengthen it. The amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) is quite unacceptable. I have spoken about it previously and indicated my reasons for saying so, and I stand by them.
It is an accepted principle of the House that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), as officers of the House, should be exempted from any restrictions on time. They will exercise their good sense in this regard and they should not be put under any such restriction. Similarly, when important legislation is introduced a Minister should not be restricted and neither should the Member replying immediately thereafter. As to other Members, we now have a 20 minute limit on speeches at the resolution stage and we will see how we get along with that.
A problem has arisen with regard to the interpretation of the provisional Standing Order dealing with the resolution stage and I think clarification is needed to show that a Member speaking for 20 minutes should not be precluded from re-entering the debate either to put a question or to continue some points he has made. It would be very difficult to limit a Member at the committee stage to 20 minutes, if that period were interpreted as being all that was allowed for his total contribution. There is general agreement on a 20 minutes limit at any one time.
I again make a strong plea to the Government that paragraph 1 of order No. 14 be separated from the rest of the resolution. There are precedents for doing this, and the arguments advanced last year in favour of the division of a resolution apply even more strongly on this occasion. The two suoject matters of allocation of time and the length of discussion on estimates are quite separate and could easily be divided.
We can accept one with but little more debate and get on with the setting up of the committees. A committee has to be set up to draft a report on the consequential
June 2, 1965

changes that will need to be made with regard to debates on estimates. That will take some time, as will the naming of the committees and their organization. It could conceivably take many weeks if we wait for the whole package deal. Therefore I suggest we divide the resolution, accept those portions which are readily acceptable to everyone, and discuss and negotiate with respect to the remainder.

speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the proposals put forward by the hon. Member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) I think we should have an answer from the Government. We are attempting to change rules by open debate, which is very good indeed but it does take up considerable time of the House. There are arguments in favour of doing it this way and arguments against.
The argument against is that when alternative proposals are put forward the Government should state either its acceptance or rejection of them so that we will know where we stand. If there is complete rejection of proposals then we can carry on debate, have a vote and impose the will of the majority.
My feeling with regard to rule changes has always been that they should be arrived at by general agreement. My experience in the past on committees dealing with the rules under the chairmanship of the Speaker was that there was general agreement before the House was asked to modify its rules. But now we seem to have gotten ourselves into a situation where a change in the rules is going to be imposed by majority unless, as I stated earlier, by talking across the floor we arrive at a consensus which is favourable to major changes.
We had quite a discussion last week on the first part of the resolution. Various modifications were agreed to as a result of the debate. There may be some reluctance here and there with regard to that portion of the changes in rules but so far as the parties are concerned there is general acceptance of an experimental process with regard to limiting the time for estimates and reducing the number of supply motions.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
That portion of this measure should be separated from the controversial part which deals with the allocation of time element. That portion should be adopted by the House so that we can get on with the setting up of
House of Commons Procedures the committees and assigning the estimates to them. Otherwise we shall continue to argue about the controversial question respecting allocation of time. I have expressed my dissent with regard to it. It is covered by a phrase which makes it palatable to those who do not understand what is going on. It is called allocation of time. In other words, this is a means toward the orderly arrangement of our business. But in actual fact it is the worst form of closure which has been devised within the system of parliamentary democracy. When I spoke on a previous occasion I pointed out that this was closure. And I am opposed to closure; I am opposed to the limitation of time as envisaged in that particular section of the resolution.
Somewhat reluctantly I went along with the idea of an over-all imposition of a time limit on consideration of the general estimates. I did not think it was necessary but I was prepared to go along with that particular change on an experimental basis. However, I continue to be opposed to this closure plan which is decked out like a sugar pill so that people will swallow it. It is suggested that a Business Committee shall meet and that the representatives of the five parties in this House should decide that there is to be a limitation of time imposed on some debate. If that did not prove satisfactory, then the Government would itself impose a limitation on the time. That is closure. We have a closure rule on the books. The proposition put forward by the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) the other night simply lifted the closure rule as it stands on our books and incorporated it into his amendment. The closure rule, once applied, limits everybody to a 20 minute speech from the period the motion comes before the House until one o'clock at night. Then the debate is over and done with. The hon. Member lifted that provision out of the present closure rule and incorporated it into his amendment.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he not be fair and say that the proposal made by my hon. friend from Greenwood did have at least one difference? Standing order 33 places a limit of 20 minutes on all those taking part in the discussion under that order. Is it not a fact that the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Greenwood provides 40 minutes for some Members?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
I do not wish to impute motives to any hon. Member, but I think the hon. Member for Greenwood was thinking
June 2, 1965

House of Commons Procedures in terms of the leader of his party or of the leaders of the other small parties. He wanted them to have 40 minutes while the rest of us in the House would be restricted to 20 minutes. It does not matter what areas or what constituencies the rest of us represent. In the opinion of the hon. Member for Greenwood, if they are not in the N.D.P. group or the Social Credit group or the Creditistes they are to be restricted to 20 minutes. The leaders of the groups I have mentioned would be allowed 40 minutes. Why this should be I do not know. What constituencies do they represent which are superior to the constituencies represented by the rest of us? I take the most serious objection to that proposition.
Of course, I objected at the time to his downgrading the Leader of the Opposition, an officer of this House, by lumping him together with the leaders of other groups in this Chamber as if he did not hold an important, indeed, an essential position in our system. The Leader of the Opposition is theoretically the alternative to the Prime Minister. We recognize that these two men are officers of this House and have a special position in it. I would resist equally a move to reduce the position of the Prime Minister. This has been done by introducing the 40 minutes proposal, 40 minutes for the Prime Minister of this country and an equal amount of time for the Leader of the New Democratic group. It does not make sense.
We look to the Prime Minister to set out the case for the Government. A great responsibility rests upon the Government in introducing legislation into the House of Commons. Governments stand or fall on their actions in this connection. Is it intended to restrict the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Government party, to 40 minutes and then give the Leader of the New Democratic Party or the Leader of the Creditiste party or the Leader of the Social Credit group 40 minutes in which to tear down his proposition? It is ridiculous and that is why I have no use for the amendment introduced by the hon. Member for Greenwood. Although he modified the closure rule by introducing this sop of 40 minutes he was actually lifting out of the rule book the closure provision.
This is the situation in which we find ourselves at the present time. It appears to me we have become deadlocked on this particular section of the proposed rule changes. I do not see much difference of opinion with regard to the other changes which will come

before the committee of the whole House but on this controversial issue we are reaching a state of deadlock and this is where negotiations are essential.
We listened last night to three Members of the Liberal party speaking on behalf of the private Members of this House and saying that if limitation of debate were allowed any such arrangement would have to include protection for the private Member. But it just cannot be done. Once debate is limited, 200 or more Members of this House are prevented from taking part. If debate is restricted to a two day period, 14 hours in all, and if 20 minutes is allowed to each speaker then 42 members could take part and 222 others would have to sit silent or leave the House or just stand up and be counted during the final vote. I am glad to see that some members of the Liberal party are now realizing that the privileges of private Members will be seriously restricted under this newfangled closure rule which the Government is attempting to introduce.
I see it is five o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking
June 2, 1965

steps to slow down the emigration of our graduate students to the United States because of the larger research opportunities and higher income levels which exist in that country and, to this end, in particular, to consider whether such object may be attained in part by:
granting an equivalent tax-free period to a successful student for each year spent on accredited postgraduate study and thereby provide our highly-trained people with an opportunity to recapture more quickly the costs incurred and the loss of earnings suffered by them during training periods.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this motion is indicated in the motion itself. Basically it is twofold. First, it is intended to provide an incentive to our graduate population to continue their training. Second, it will provide an incentive to postgraduate students to remain in Canada or, if they take their postgraduate training in the United States, to return to Canada in order to take advantage of a tax-free period.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
You may ask, Mr. Speaker, why we in Canada should create such a privileged group in our society. In reply I can marshal many arguments, some of them which are included in the motion. For example, there is the shortening of earning period of someone who spends a large number of years in academic training. I could also indicate the great need for research scientists, university staff and other research workers in what is going to be a very large expansion of our university facilities in the very near future. This expansion, as many members know, is already under way and many universities are already facing a serious staffing problem in respect of the additional facilities for our expanding university population.
I think we would all agree, Mr. Speaker, that the future of Canada lies with our young population. As a small country we have to develop special skills and specialized industries if we are to compete in today's world. It seems to me that we must develop our human resources to the maximum possible degree and must take some steps to retain our most talented people instead of seeing them leave the country to take advantage of greater opportunities, particularly south of the border.
I would suggest that the new frontier for Canadians to explore is that of research and new technology. We in Canada have few products which can be truly identified, at least readily, as Canadian. We have not been able to develop those industries which are uniquely Canadian and which in my opinion will come about only by developing special
Aid to Postgraduate Students skills and industries. This we must do if we in Canada are to survive in this very materialistic world.
It is my opinion that in Canada the Federal Government particularly must play a much greater role in research by providing direct assistance to research in Canada if we are to achieve these goals. The structure of our industry is in my opinion partly responsible for the lack of uniquely Canadian industries or Canadian products. This is partly due at least to the parent-subsidiary relationship which dominates our entire economic structure. It seems to me that Canada more than any other western industrialized nation requires the Government to play a larger role if we are to meet the objectives to which 1 referred a few moment ago.
Salary opportunities in the United States are generally higher than here, but I suggest that the big draw in the main for our postgraduate students in going south of the border is the research opportunities which are provided by some industrial companies but principally at universities owing to the large funds available for research in the United States at those institutions. In comparison, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion we are poor country cousins in this field, and perhaps this accounts in greatest part for the so-called brain drain which we have been experiencing in recent years. Perhaps many Members could quote statistics to show that the net emigration-immigration balance has been somewhat in our favour, but I would suggest that the most talented people, such as postgraduate students and so on, have on the whole been lost to Canada rather than gained by Canada and certainly in some particular fields we have lost much more than we have gained.
I would refer, for instance, to the medical field where I think we are rapidly heading toward second or third class medicine in Canada unless something is done and done very soon to reverse the trend and meet the competition which through U.S. funds is attracting our most talented researchers in this particular field. This is true in other areas too. I could refer to particular industries, such as some of the industries connected with space technology, aviation and so on, where again I think we would find that in these exciting new areas loss of skilled people has certainly been a very serious hindrance to the development of our own economy and to the specialized and sophisticated industries which are likely to become the growth industries of the future.
June 2, 1965

Aid to Postgraduate Students
I am also appalled to learn of the amount of United States funds spent in this country on research. I do not for a moment suggest that we should not accept this money, but it does seem to me that there has been too great a reliance in Canada on U.S. support for research programs at some of our universities, particularly in the medical field. When the recent United States restrictions on dollar exports came into effect about a year ago there was almost panic in some of our medical research colleges because of the threat to their programs which were under way at that time. Fortunately I think we have in large measure escaped that immediate threat, but it certainly demonstrated in no uncertain fashion the acuteness of the problem to which I am referring today.
Last January I had an opportunity to meet with a number of members of the Canadian Society for Clinical Investigation, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that they are greatly concerned about the lack of Government support in Canada for medical research. I think it would be rather altruistic for us to feel that this support for medical research or for any other kind of research in Canada is going to come from other sources than the Federal Government. The basic problem, as I see it and as I indicated earlier, is the parent-subsidiary relationship which we have in our industrial society, which has pretty well meant that most of the research done by these organizations, in many cases international organizations, is going to be done by the parent company and is likely to result in the development of products which are going to be identified largely as United States products. Thus under these conditions in no way can we hope to achieve any kind of specialized industries emanating out of research.
Getting back to the problems in the medical field, we are now talking of medicare as an urgent social need in Canada. I am one of those who support that view. But only a cursory examination of the whole plan reveals that medicare may be almost impossible without considerable expansion of our medical colleges and the staff to man them. In this particular field especially, Mr. Speaker, I think it can be said that university staff and research people are synonymous. The only way you can get an adequate medical staff of top calibre is to provide extensive research facilities in order to keep these people in the academic world. They obviously can make much more money by practising their professions than by teaching. If we are to compete
[Mr. Moreau.l
with the tremendous United States programs, with almost unlimited funds for the support of medical research in one form or another, we must begin to thing seriously in this regard.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
This whole problem in respect of a research policy in Canada as it applies to the medical profession is one of the most pressing with which we are now faced. It is not my belief that the proposal I have made to the House today will provide a coherent or dynamic research policy in Canada. However, if this measure is adopted this in itself would indicate and recognize the fact that we consider this to be an urgent problem and that we are willing to tackle it immediately at some level.
One might very well ask how this proposal could work. If one of our postgraduate students was weighing the advantages of a position in the United States against a similar position in Canada, the immediate advantage of a tax-free period for each year spent on postgraduate study would have a tremendous bearing. I should point out immediately that all our Government assistance programs in education are available only at the graduate level. An immediate tax advantage during a period of perhaps three or four years would carry considerable weight.
Naturally if an individual had taken his postgraduate studies at M.I.T. or some other United States university he would have to come to Canada and remain for at least three or four years in order to obtain such an advantage. It is my contention that such a student having lived here for four or five years would have developed some roots, some seniority rights, some advancement in the company for which he worked and would probably have married, with the result that his mobility would be considerably lessened. On that assumption I feel that my proposal has some merit and that it might work.
It certainly would provide incentive to many of our graduate students to go on to postgraduate work. In fact, it would also provide an incentive to some of our graduates who are now working to go back to university for specialized training in specialized skills. Those individuals would then be able to make a considerable contribution to our economy.
We do have special considerations in respect of our tax laws, for instance, for wasting assets, particularly in the case of mining taxation. We provide a three year tax-free period for new mines coming into production as an incentive to people to develop these
June 2, 1965

resources and as partial compensation for the wasting assets they have. I would ask hon. Members to consider that perhaps a fully trained man is now in the same category as a wasting asset and that perhaps a special tax consideration of this kind would not be out of order.
Another argument I might put forward is that, while I am not a particular admirer of the Russian way of life, we must recognize that Russia has achieved a considerable measure of progress by setting up something of a special status for engineers, scientists, artists and other talented people. In other words, an individual who comes within that privileged group in that society is an individual who has developed special skills. These special privileges can be considered as incentives in that society which can perhaps be regarded as not a free society. I think we must admit that they have attained a considerable degree of progress in certain fields. I feel, therefore, that this proposal is not too far out of line.
I do not intend to speak very much longer and I should like to remind hon. Members of the House that a message has been received from the other place in respect of Royal Assent at 5.45. I hope they will keep that fact in mind during the remaining time available in order that the question can be put to the House before then.
The final point I should like to make relates to the cost of such a concession. The cost would not be high as we are not dealing with a great number of people in our economy, and if we weigh the contributions that those people can make to our economy, in relation to the cost this proposal, I suggest, has a great deal of merit. My final thought is that we have spent a great deal of taxation dollars on individuals by the time they have finished postgraduate training. We have contributed to their education through public funds during grade school, high school, university and postgraduate training. For that reason I believe we should adopt this proposal in order to protect that investment.

Mr. Speaker, I shall certainly be heedful of the hon. Member's suggestion regarding brevity. It is too bad he wasted it on me because I am always brief, although perhaps not as brief as I myself think I am! I will not utilize one-third of an hour as he has done. But I do not hesitate to add that he used the time advantageously.
I appreciate the hon. Member's views and I compliment him for bringing forward this 22620-123
Aid to Postgraduate Students very interesting suggestion. The brain drain problem, as we all know, is not a new one. I suppose a country such as ours, in proximity to a larger, more wealthy and more populous country, would naturally suffer from the compelling forces which emanate from that larger entity, and certainly they come very strongly to the people with skilled training and higher education.
While it is not usually wise to use the expression "crisis", nor any other emotionally loaded word, too casually, I think we can say at the present time we do face in all areas of education in the country something of a crisis. Our universities are encountering the largest population potential of students ever. More graduates were turned out this year than ever before. More of them will wish to go on to postgraduate work, but not all of them will be able to do so.
The hon. Member's suggestion is a good one, and if I had any criticism of it it would be that it is somewhat inadequate in view of the immensity of the problem. I certainly support it. I intend to conclude my remarks so there will be time to vote on this resolution, and I will vote for it.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
We will never be able to resist completely the strong pull to the south. It will take many, many years to bring about a situation in which our universities are able to offer to graduate students the kind of things which are offered by institutions such as Harvard and Yale. Many of our graduates do go south to obtain their postgraduate training and often they do not come back for the reason that the institution in which they take their higher degrees, having spotted their capacity, will immediately draw them to its bosom, because they have all sorts of research projects and opportunities in their larger and wealthier universities which we are not able to provide here.
I believe we are going to find it increasingly necessary for the Dominion Government to be helpful in this field. There were certain things done in the income tax field a few years ago which helped in this respect. National Housing Act legislation was introduced which benefited our universities. There are a number of things which the Dominion Government can do and there are a great many more things it must do. It has seemed to be the pattern that helpful participation by the Dominion Government is more readily accepted the higher you go in the educational level.
I noted what the hon. Member said about United States funds. There were times when
1916	COMMONS
Aid to Postgraduate Students postgraduate students, especially in the social sciences, a field in which I am most interested, would, if it were not for the largesse of American institutions and foundations, have found the going very hard. What the Rockefeller, Ford, and Carnegie Foundations have done for Canadian scholarship is a long and glorious story and they deserve the greatest credit. We have had some recent difficulties in that some institutions of this kind in the United States feel that the Canada Council should be filling the gap. Some of our students have encountered difficulty there.
It is a matter that has always concerned me-it is not within the ambit of this resolution but I would like to mention it in passing and I think those of us who are interested in education must always mention it-that the Canadian record of individual and private largesse does not compare at all favourably with that of the United States. There are a few Lord Beaverbrooks but not so many, and we do not have the great private foundations which can be of such assistance in this respect. There is too much of a tendency to leave it all to the Canada Council. It is interesting that some people who philosophically often impress upon you their views that the Government that does least is the best Government will, in a case of this kind, be quite content to leave it to some quasi-govemmental agency.
I think the hon. Member, in his discussion of the National Research Council, has a good point, too. I do not know what is intended in the upcoming legislation; I cannot understand what is going to be done there. But I hope it will result in an enlargement of the National Research Council. It should be able to do a great deal more in the field of encouragement of and assistance to postgraduate training. I must also point out that we are still requiring greater emphasis upon the social sciences rather than the natural and physical sciences.
I listened carefully to what the hon. Member said, and if there had been anything with which I could have disagreed, I would have disagreed briefly. But I commend the hon. Member for this step, this thought. I see no reason why anyone should regard this as setting up an improperly privileged class in our society, and indeed I agree with him that this small measure would add, I think significantly, to the training and developing of our great human resources, because we shall need them as never before. The demand for teachers and professors alone is staggering as one projects the requirements of the next few years. Of course, all these facilities cost money; libraries, and laboratories cost money
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
DEBATES	June 2, 1965
and there are tremendous demands of many kinds.
I would congratulate the hon. Member and would hope that this is just one idea which will be accepted. I cannot refer to other items on the order paper, but I am very pleased that in this session there have been a number of matters such as that raised by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) which show a wholesome and intelligent interest in this problem of how best to utilize the natural ability of our young people. I commend the hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, and support his point of view wholeheartedly.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Would the hon. gentleman say that we should do more to encourage private benefaction? The Americans, to whom the hon. Member referred, and the British have done so much for scholarship and are doing a great deal in the way of offering inducements to increase private benefaction. Does the hon. Member think that our tax laws should be so fashioned as to encourage foundations?
I certainly do, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak very briefly in support of the resolution before us, limited and inadequate as it may be. Many observers have deplored for many years the loss to Canada of many of its young people who have been going to the United States for their training and employment. In fairness, however, I think we should remember that through the years Canadian universities and industries have been built by immigrants from many parts of the world. A visit to any campus or any large industrial enterprise will confirm this fact. Canada would be a poor place if we were dependant entirely upon native sons to build these enterprises in education and business. However, Mr. Speaker, I think we would all agree that no young Canadian should be obliged to leave home because of lack of opportunity to be trained or employed. To avoid this I suggest three improvements which might be made at once, apart from the one contained in the resolution.
First, reduce the cost of attending university today. This is something that could be done within a few hours if this House made up its mind and was given leadership by the Government. I have in mind that at the University of British Columbia
June 2, 1965

just last week the President told the students that the planned increase in fees would not be made if the per capita grant to universities across Canada was increased from $2 to $3 per person. I am quite certain that the announced increase in university fees in various universities across Canada would not be made and would not be continued for the rest of this year if the Government were to act at once in increasing the per capita grant right across this country.
Second, improve the research facilities in industries and universities. Students do complain about the poorer facilities in Canada compared with those in the United States. This applies not only to public institutions supported by the Government of Canada but also to the facilities supplied by private industry.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Third, provide the latest information to students wherever they may be in the world. In support of this last contention, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote an editorial entitled, "Plugging the 'Brain Drain' ", which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of December 14, 1964:
There would be fewer plaintive Canadian cries about the "brain drain" from this country if others showed the same initiative as President Murray G. Ross of York University in seeking out expatriate Canadians.
In a recent speech in Toronto Mr. Ross told of a trip to the University of California where he arranged to meet the Canadian students doing graduate study. Of the 147 Canadian graduate students at the university more than 100 came to hear Mr. Ross and bombard him with questions about Canada.
Here was Mr. Ross' conclusion:
"It seemed to me that these students were saying that because they had little contact with Canada, because few people or organizations seemed interested in their return to Canada, and because there seemed to be small assurance of adequate research grants for young scholars in Canada.. . they tended to look with favour on job offers in the United States."
Mr. Ross reported the students as saying that almost all the job offers came from the United States and the few coming from Canada arrive "very late in the academic year-after their decision for the year ahead has been made."
"The only contact with Canada all seem to have," he said, "is a questionnaire sent to them by the Federal Government. None were impressed by this form."
Not much in all this indicates that Canada is really concerned about the loss of specially trained persons. If the universities need teachers as badly as they say they do or if industry is really looking for highly qualified personnel, they should be haunting places like the University of California...
Most Canadian students go to American schools because of the specialized courses available or to accept scholarships. Most intend to return home.
Aid to Postgraduate Students
But they lose touch quickly and too many will be permanently lost to Canada unless those who need their talents have enough initiative to attract them back.
Considering the variety of things you get in Canada, it should not be too difficult for the Government to arrange for some public agency to keep Canadian youth, wherever they may be in the world, informed regarding opportunities for training and employment in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to be brief, but I am glad to support the views put forth by the hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau), to the effect that scientists or specialists constitute a strong asset for a country such as Canada and that all possible steps should be taken to keep them in this country.
I do not think his motion is designed to prevent other scientists or specialists from settling in Canada, but, on the other hand, we are just as anxious as anybody else to keep all our talented people in Canada by offering them interesting proposals and conditions.
The main task of our universities consists in supplying the Canadian market with the brains it needs, and not foreign markets in the large proportion prevailing at the present time. The suggestions of the hon. Member for York-Scarborough might provide a solution to this problem, but in the course of a study or of the application of legislation concerning this problem, other solutions would, certainly be found. I feel that the mere suggestion of this solution by the hon. Member for York-Scarborough is already a step forward.
Some thought should also be given to the instillation into our students of very strong national and patriotic feelings in order to make them realize the urgency of putting their talents at the service of their country, in the first place, and indirectly, of all mankind. It must be admitted, however, that patriotic feelings alone are not sufficient to keep in our country all our talented people, because as the Latin proverb goes: Primo vivere, delude philosophari-that is, let us live first, and then indulge in philosophy.
I feel that the required means should be sought as soon as possible because the more we delay, the more our talented people will emigrate to foreign countries. The passage of this motion will enable us to find other means in addition to those suggested by the hon. member for York-Scarborough, and then we

Aid to Postgraduate Students shall perhaps be proud to have succeeded in putting a stop to this brain drain.
It should be kept in mind, however, that since education comes under provincial jurisdiction, there should be no infringement on provincial autonomy in the solution of this problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
First, I should like personally to congratulate the hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) for developing this resolution. I think his is a particularly ingenius way of helping to stop the brain drain from Canada. Personally, I am going to lay this measure, along with some others, before the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) for his serious consideration in connection with his budget for next year.
I think, too, that because of the widespread interest in the subject of research and development, and more particularly in respect of keeping gifted, educated young Canadians in Canada, we might well recommend that this subject be referred to one of the new Committees which will be set up under the new regulations with regard to procedure. We should have an opportunity to call before such a Committee the members of the new science secretariat. The committee could also send for other people across Canada who can be expected to express considered views as to the course of research and development in this country and the contribution which it could best make to our economy.
In looking over the motion proposed by the hon. Member for York-Scarborough, I noticed that he outlined several of the root causes for this brain drain. One is the relatively high level of income in the United States, that is, the higher level of income available to engineers and scientists. The other is the larger research opportunities in that country. Both of these reasons are basically economic ones. In other words, if we solve some of our economic problems we will be able to stem the brain drain and, vice-versa, the retention of this body of gifted knowledge in Canada will, of course, help improve our economic lot.
I should like to point out that the general consensus amongst economists these days is that the growth of an economy is due to two substantial factors. One is an increase in population, the employee working force, in effect, and the other is an increase in productivity. Most economists now also agree that

DEBATES	June 2, 1965
the increase in productivity is due mainly to new and better ideas. The industry of ideas, in other words, is perhaps equal to population growth as a force for expansion in a modern economy. Scientists, engineers and technicians are therefore vital to the growth of our Canadian economy. We must attract as many as we can from other countries. We must keep as many home as we can. We must bring back those graduates who take advanced degrees in other countries in order to increase our rate of productivity and improve the efficiency of our economy, as well as see that it expands as a result of population growth.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Our effort in this country must be directed along economic lines. I am referring specifically to expenditures in respect of research and development. I believe we should channel some part of our research and development expenditures into industries which are the bread and butter industries of the nation, industries which are today the most productive, industries which show the greatest growth prospects for the future. We must, in other words, reinforce success rather than spread our efforts across the entire spectrum of industry, across the entire field of research and development activity. We must call our shots. We must do this not only in respect of individual industries but we must also pay attention to the regional aspects of research and development. We must recognize the results of experience in other countries. The experience there is that you have a few large science based complexes in operation, not dozens of small establishments scattered far and wide.
This is true, for instance, in the United States. In the Boston area around the Massachusetts Institutute of Technology you have not only university research facilities and government financed laboratories but also science oriented industries. You have the three major institutional aspects of development and there is an interplay of ideas and an exchange of information and knowledge between these three major institutions -the universities or the centres of education, the government research laboratories and the private firms which are interested basically in the profit motive.
Out in California you have a similar development at Stanford where you have universities and businesses and governments all acting together. In this country we are about
June 2, 1965

to make a start so we too must decide what areas should be backed up in respect of research.
I personally decry the decentralization of some of our government research establishments. They should be around the principal university areas. They should be in areas where industry is already research oriented. As a specific example, I do not think that the Forest Products Laboratory, now located in the constituency of the hon. Member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau), should be moved to Sault Ste. Marie. I think it should probably be expanded but located in close proximity to an area where there are one or more universities and a considerable industrial base. It is through this practical approach to research and development that we are likely to become more proficient in producing new ideas, new methods and new products in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Perhaps I should yield the floor to other hon. Members who are expressing ideas from their seats, but may I be permitted one or two minutes in which to wind up my remarks?
The Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) has made several significant speeches on research and development. He has given us many statistics comparing our industrial research and development effort with that of other more industrialized nations, and we appear to a considerable disadvantage in these comparisons. We have to step up our industrial research and development effort by a multiple of six in order to equate the present per capita level in countries like the United Kingdom and the United States. We have to put more emphasis on applied research as distinct from basic research. I do not mean to imply that we should cut back the expenditure that we are making in respect of Government research, pure research, by such institutions as the National Research Council. This should expand by, say, 10 per cent a year or in line with that of other countries, but in order to catch up in the applied field, the practical field of development, we have to step up our industrial research.
We have also to step up research in our universities. We have to step it up to a rate of about 20 per cent per annum and maintain it over a period of years in order to get it into a balanced relationship akin to that in industrially advanced countries.
Aid to Postgraduate Students
We must shift the emphasis of Government expenditure. Today over 80 per cent of our money goes into pure, fundamental research with no direct application to our economy. Less than 10 per cent goes to industry and less than 10 per cent to the universities. This relationship must be changed. It must be changed with something like 40 per cent going to basic research, with the rest to applied research in industry and in the universities. We must also develop science oriented complexes where the universities, industries and the Government research establishments are located side by side.
We cannot have dozens of them to begin with. We can only have a few and we must be selective. We must make difficult decisions in this connection. Only in this way will we be able to keep those young people at home who have been trained at public expense and who drift to other countries to seize opportunities there.
I think I have proven quite conclusively, especially in respect of my remarks on economic growth, that we can forgo the income tax that these young people will not have to pay if the recommendation of the hon. Member for York-Scarborough were to be accepted by the Minister of Finance.
